flashcards.q: Give the minute-by-minute allocation for a 45-minute design round.
flashcards.a: 0-2 restate and declare the plan; 2-5 requirements; 5-8 estimation; 8-22 high-level breadth end to end; 22 checkpoint; 22-40 deep dives; 40-45 close. Deep-dive weight dominates the rubric while most candidates spend ~60% of the round on the high-level diagram.

flashcards.q: What are the four axes an interviewer scores, and where is the failure asymmetry?
flashcards.a: Scoping (did they define the problem or wait for it), Communication (could I follow it without knowing the answer), Technical depth (did they go below the name of the technology), Tradeoffs and judgment (did they choose or just list). Asymmetry: you can pass with a mediocre architecture and excellent reasoning; you cannot pass with an excellent architecture the interviewer could not follow.

flashcards.q: What is the test for whether a clarifying question is worth asking?
flashcards.a: Would a different answer change your architecture? 'How many users' changes it. 'What is the exact SLA in milliseconds' usually does not, so state your assumption instead. Ask three or four questions, not ten; past about four minutes the interviewer starts wondering whether you can make a decision.

flashcards.q: What must an estimation phase output, beyond a number?
flashcards.a: A design constraint. End with a sentence of the form 'which tells me the design problem is ___'. Estimation whose output is a number is a calculation; estimation whose output is a constraint is engineering.

flashcards.q: Give the seven-step structure of one deep dive.
flashcards.a: 1) Name the problem precisely. 2) State the constraint. 3) Give two or three real options. 4) Choose, with the reason. 5) State the cost you accept. 6) Go one level below the choice. 7) VOLUNTEER the failure mode, unprompted. Step 7 is what separates staff from senior.
'A or B. I'd take A, because [property of THIS problem]. What I'm giving up is C.' Once per deep dive, add: 'the argument for the other side is ___, and it wins if ___.'

flashcards.q: What is the single strongest juniority signal, and the rule that prevents it?
flashcards.a: Jargon density: naming technologies in rapid succession without grounding them in the specific problem, which reads as performing knowledge rather than applying it. Rule: every technology you name gets a 'because [this problem]' in the SAME sentence. No orphan nouns.

flashcards.q: What is wrong with answering 'it depends', and what is the fix?
flashcards.a: It is correct and useless; all the information is in what it depends on. Fix: 'It depends on the read-write ratio. If reads dominate, X; if writes, Y.' Name the variable and both branches.

flashcards.q: Give the four-step answer to 'how would you scale this', and which step nobody does.
flashcards.a: 1) Ask what is scaling: users, data, or requests per user. 2) Name the component that breaks first and why. 3) Name the observable SYMPTOM, not just the cause (p99 up, error rate flat, queue time growing faster than compute). 4) Give the fix, then what breaks next. Step 3 is the one almost nobody does and it proves you have operated a system rather than only designed one.

flashcards.q: Give the six-step recovery script for a wrong turn, and say which step matters most.
flashcards.a: Stop mid-sentence; name it ('let me back up, I don't think that works'); SAY WHY in your own words; give the fix; name the new cost; move on without over-apologising. Step 3 matters most: 'you're right, let me change it' scores as compliance, 'you're right, and the reason it doesn't work is X' scores as understanding.

flashcards.q: How do you tell whether to hold your position or update when the interviewer pushes back?
flashcards.a: If they present NEW INFORMATION ('what if the write rate is 100x the read rate'), update. If they only apply PRESSURE ('are you sure?'), restate your reasoning once and name what would change your mind. On a second push, take it seriously regardless. Defending past the second signal is disqualifying; folding on the first is nearly as bad.

flashcards.q: What are the three signals that you are on a wrong turn?
flashcards.a: 1) The interviewer asks the same question a second time in different words: they are steering, not curious. 2) 'Are you sure that works?' or 'walk me through what happens when...': a hint, not a question. 3) They go quiet and stop writing.

flashcards.q: How do you present architecture with no whiteboard?
flashcards.a: Number the components, state direction explicitly since there are no arrows, and name them once so both of you reuse the same vocabulary. 'There are four components. One, an edge service... The request goes edge, then fans out in parallel to two and three.' Then check in before going deeper. Netflix and some staff loops run with no diagramming tool at all.

flashcards.q: What are the four elements of a close, at minute 40?
flashcards.a: What you built; why the key decision was made; what you know is unfinished; what you would do next. Naming your own gaps at the close demonstrates calibration and interviewers write it down. Never let the round end by running out of clock.

flashcards.q: What is the checkpoint sentence at minute 22, and what four things does it do?
flashcards.a: 'That's the whole system end to end. I think the two most interesting problems are X and Y. I'd start with X because I think it's the actual bottleneck. Would you rather I go there, or somewhere else?' It declares breadth complete, demonstrates prioritisation, makes a recommendation rather than only a menu, and hands over control briefly.

flashcards.q: Why is explaining fundamentals penalised at staff level, and how do you calibrate?
flashcards.a: Your interviewer is a staff-plus engineer who already knows most of what you would explain, so exhaustive coverage reads as failing to calibrate. Watch them: nodding without writing means wrong altitude. The move is to compress the known and expand the specific: 'you know how a cache works, so let me go straight to the invalidation question.'

flashcards.q: 'Could you do this with a single machine?' Why is this a trap and how do you answer?
flashcards.a: It tests whether you over-engineer by default. Often the answer is yes: at 100 rps peak with 2.5 GB of vectors a single well-provisioned instance handles it, and you distribute for availability and deployment independence rather than for capacity. Be explicit about which reason is the real one. Candidates who cannot justify their own distribution are marked down.

flashcards.q: You have not mentioned monitoring. What are the right signals, and what do you alert on versus dashboard?
flashcards.a: Name signals that detect YOUR failure modes: queue time separately from total latency, cache hit rate, the silent-failure counter (fallback or unresolved rate), cost per request. Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency SLO burn) that need human action; dashboard the rest. Cause-based alerts on CPU page you for things that do not matter and miss things that do.
